prompt: An analyst retypes OKONO's inventory with every capex and the limit as a count of USD where they were million USD, and changes nothing else. What changes in how the engine solves it, and where would the analyst see the change?
options: The optimizer switches to its fallback grid, since a limit in the hundreds of millions holds more partial portfolios than the exact solve allows.
The engine refuses the run with a PortfolioInputError, since a capex that large beside NPVs in million USD fails the engine's scale check.
Nothing in the solve or the output: the same funded set comes back, because the knapsack is exact at any scale.
The grid stays at 1 million USD per cell but every project now weighs a million times more cells, so none of them fits under the limit and nothing is funded at all.
explanation: Read at their typed precision, the retyped figures give the same knapsack scaled by a million, so OKONO still funds OK-1 + OK-3 + OK-4 for 291.0000. A unit slip is visible only in the inputs a reviewer reads.
why: Keyed grid switch is false: the solve is exact in any unit (rawDollars); option 0 became true for a wrong reason. Copy rule: contrastive ("instead of", "rather than", ", never", ", not") reworded, meaning unchanged.

prompt: A risky project's chance of success is left out of its row entirely. Beyond its risked EMV, what does the default do to the seeded risk summary of a set that funds it?
options: Nothing, since the simulation draws its own success rate from the entered percentiles whatever pos says, and only the optimizer uses the default.
The default of 1 travels into the simulation, so the project succeeds in every iteration, adds no failure to P(loss) and does not drag down the P90.
The simulation refuses to run for that set and reports P(loss) as null until a chance of success is entered for every funded project.
The simulation treats the blank as a coin toss and draws success half the time, so the set looks riskier than its risked EMV would suggest.
explanation: A pos left out or null is the default 1, used everywhere the project is used; at seed 20260829 and 10000 iterations the project is a certain success. A pos typed as a blank is refused by name before anything runs.
why: A blank pos is refused; only a pos left out defaults to 1. Prompt now says left out. Copy rule: contrastive ("instead of", "rather than", ", never", ", not") reworded, meaning unchanged.

prompt: A study already paid for elsewhere is added to OKONO as a project with capex 0.0000 and a positive risked EMV, and the limit stays at 450.0000. Can the engine's answer hold it together with OK-1 + OK-3 + OK-4?
options: No: the optimizer keeps the set it has already found for 450.0000 and adds nothing to a limit that is fully spent.
Yes, but only with overLimit true and overLimitBy of 1 million USD, since the engine lets a free project squeeze in over a limit that is already spent.
Yes: a project with capex 0.0000 weighs nothing on the exact solve, so it is funded beside OK-1 + OK-3 + OK-4 whenever its risked EMV is positive.
No, because a capex of 0.0000 is refused by the check that stops a negative capex.
explanation: On the exact solve a free project weighs nothing: freeProjectTightLimit funds free + A at capex 100.0000 for 70.0000 at a limit of 100.0000, and freeProjectZeroLimit funds the free project even at a limit of 0.0000.
why: Free projects weigh nothing on the exact solve; the old key is false and option 0 was the truth.

prompt: Two answers leave money idle: OKONO at 750.0000 spends 690.0000, and the gridUndershootFallback case, run on the stated fallback grid, spends 4500.0000 of 6000.0000. Why is only the second a reason to look harder at the set?
options: The second leaves a quarter of its limit idle and the first under a tenth, and the engine marks an answer unreliable once idle money passes a set share of the limit.
OKONO is solved exactly and its one left-out project, OK-6 at 310.0000, cannot fit, while the fallback rounds weights up and states optimalityGap 200.0000, the most its set may leave out.
The fallback reports overLimit true, which marks a grid problem, while OKONO at 750.0000 reports false and so needs no further check by the reader.
Both are equally suspect, since money left unspent always means the knapsack stopped early and a better set of whole projects exists somewhere.
explanation: On gridUndershootFallback the weights of 500, 500, 500 and 501 cells exceed 2000, so the fallback funds X + Y + Z for 660.0000 with solveMethod grid-feasible, while W at 1499.0000 fits in money and the exact optimum is 860.0000. OKONO's 60.0000 is genuine because nothing that remains fits.
why: gridUndershoot is solved exactly; the undershoot lives only on the stated fallback, which reports optimalityGap.

prompt: In tieDifferentComposition the engine returns A for 80.0000 where B + C also reaches 80.0000. What would a reviewer need in order to compare the P(loss) of the two sets?
options: A separate simulation of B + C, because the engine's risk summary covers only the set it returned and its output names no alternative optimum.
Nothing extra, since the risk summary averages P(loss) over every set that ties on risked EMV and reports the blended figure beside the funded set.
Nothing extra, since tied sets share their risked EMV and therefore share their P(loss) and their P90 as well, whatever projects they hold.
A rerun on a finer grid, since the engine lists alternative optima in its output only when the resolution drops below 1.0000.
explanation: Among sets tied on risked EMV the optimizer keeps the one with less capex, and at equal capex the set built without the later project in the list; A and B + C both cost 100.0000, so A comes back. A is one bet and B + C spreads the same 80.0000 over two, so their risk can differ widely.
why: Tie rule stated as it is: less capex first, then the set built without the later project.

prompt: Three inventories each hide a problem: a capex typed as -150, a pos typed as 1.4, and a large inventory sent to the stated fallback grid, which leaves out a project worth 200.0000. How does the engine treat each?
options: It refuses all three, because each one breaks a condition the knapsack needs before it can honestly return a set under the limit.
It refuses the first, reads the second as 1 and funds that project as a certain success, and flags the third through overLimit.
It refuses the first, reads the second as the default of 1, and reports the third as money unspent with nothing else beside it.
It refuses the first two by project name, and reports the third with solveMethod "grid-feasible" and an optimalityGap of 200.0000.
explanation: The messages read Project "B" has a negative capex (-150); capex must be 0 or more, and Project "a" has a pos outside 0 to 1 (1.4); pos must be a number from 0 to 1. On gridUndershootFallback the fallback funds X + Y + Z for 660.0000 and states the bound beside it.
why: Two premises no longer occur on the exact solve; rebuilt on a pos refusal and the fallback optimalityGap.

prompt: Working a graded inventory, a candidate finds the result reports solveMethod "grid-feasible". What does the Associate method require before the funded set is quoted?
options: Nothing extra, since the fallback rounds every weight up and a set that fits its grid can only be the exact optimum.
Rerun with a smaller limit until solveMethod reads "exact", since the engine offers its exact solve on request once asked.
Read its optimalityGap, 200.0000 on gridUndershootFallback, as the most risked EMV the set may leave out, and look for a left-out project that still fits in money.
Confirm overLimit reads false, since the fallback can only go wrong by overshooting the limit and the flag reports every overshoot.
explanation: The fallback rounds every weight up, so its set always fits the limit; it can fall short of the optimum, and optimalityGap states how far at most: 20.0000 on gridOvershootFallback, where nothing was lost, and 200.0000 on gridUndershootFallback, where W was left out.
why: Resolution is null on an exact solve; the check keys on solveMethod and optimalityGap.

prompt: A report shows OKONO's frontier ending at 450.0000 and 291.0000 beside a funded set worth 287.7500. What should the reader conclude?
options: The funded set is the greedy set and the frontier is the optimum, which the engine prints side by side so the loss can be seen.
The grid has undershot, and the 3.2500 between them is a project rounding left out.
The two were not run on the same inventory and limit, so find which input changed before quoting either.
The frontier includes projects the funded set excludes for risk, so its last point always sits a little above the set.
explanation: The last point is the best risked EMV inside the whole limit and must match the funded set; at 450.0000 both read OK-1 + OK-3 + OK-4 for 291.0000, solved exactly with solveMethod "exact".
why: No resolution on an exact solve.

prompt: gridOvershootFallback, run on the stated fallback grid, reports a resolution of 3.000000 at a limit of 6000.0000. What does a resolution measure?
options: The size of one capex cell in the money units entered, the limit divided into 2000 cells, reported only when the fallback grid runs.
The precision of the risked EMV, so the answer is reliable only to within 3.000000 million USD of the true optimum.
The number of cells the limit is divided into, which grows when the capexes are typed in larger units.
The standard error of the simulated P(loss), which the engine shrinks as the limit grows.
explanation: 6000.0000 over 2000 is 3.000000 million USD per cell, and every capex is rounded up to whole cells, A to 1334, B to 668 and C to 665. On an exact solve the resolution is null, because there is no grid.
why: rawDollars and nonIntegerLimit report resolution null; a resolution exists only on the fallback grid.

prompt: On gridOvershootFallback the stated fallback grid runs at 3.000000 per cell against a limit of 6000.0000, with A at 4000.0000, B at 2002.0000 and C at 1995.0000. Why are A and B never funded together there?
options: The fallback funds at most two of any three projects, and keeps the pair with the lower total capex.
Every capex rounds up to whole cells, B to 668, so A's 1334 and B's 668 overflow the 2000 cells, and the fallback funds A + C for 780.0000.
The fallback refuses any project whose capex does not divide evenly by the resolution, and B's 2002.0000 is refused.
A is charged the minimum of one cell as a large project, so the grid undercounts it by nearly its whole capex of 4000.0000.
explanation: Rounding every weight up keeps any set that fits the grid inside the limit. The fallback funds A + C at 5995.0000, the exact optimum, with overLimit false and optimalityGap 20.0000.
why: gridOvershoot is exact; the fallback rounds weights up so A and B cannot both fit.

prompt: gridOvershootFallback reports optimalityGap 20.0000 and gridUndershootFallback 200.0000. What does each gap say about the fallback's set?
options: Both mean the grid was coarse by that many cells, the figure recording how many capexes were rounded up.
Each is exactly the risked EMV the fallback lost, so the first case lost 20.0000 and the second lost 200.0000.
Each is the amount by which the funded capex sits over the limit, reported beside overLimit for the reader to subtract.
Each is an upper bound on what was left out: the first set is the exact optimum at 780.0000, while the second falls 200.0000 short.
explanation: optimalityGap is the optimum on the same grid with every weight rounded down, less the funded EMV. On gridOvershootFallback that bound admits A + B, yet A + C is the exact optimum; on gridUndershootFallback X + Y + Z at 660.0000 falls short of all four at 860.0000 by exactly the gap.
why: Both golden cases are exact now; the gap question moves to optimalityGap on the two fallbacks.

prompt: A capital committee cannot see why the four gridUndershoot candidates, whose capex totals 5999.0000 against a limit of 6000.0000, are never funded together on the stated fallback of gridUndershootFallback. What stops the fourth there?
options: The engine caps a funded set at three projects on a coarse grid, which keeps the knapsack inside its time budget.
Z's 1502.0000 is refused as over a per-project ceiling of 1500.0000, and the grid drops W with it as the least valuable.
On a cell of 3.000000 every capex rounds up, and the four rounded weights need more than the 2000 cells the limit holds.
The four together would overshoot in money, so the overshoot flag removes the cheapest project before the answer is reported.
explanation: W, X and Y weigh 500 cells each and Z 501, one cell more than 2000; the fallback funds X + Y + Z for 660.0000 and states optimalityGap 200.0000. Solved exactly, gridUndershoot funds all four for 860.0000.
why: gridUndershoot funds all four exactly; only the fallback leaves one out.

prompt: Between freeProjectTightLimit and freeProjectSlack the only change is one extra million of limit, and both fund the free project and A. What does the extra million buy?
options: The free project's capex, which the engine rounds up from 0.0000 to 1 million USD whenever a limit allows it.
Nothing: both fund capex 100.0000 for 70.0000, and the extra 1.0000 is left unspent.
A change of method, since a limit of 101.0000 sends the solve to the fallback grid.
A tie the engine breaks by entry order, which the extra million settles in the free project's favour.
explanation: A free project weighs nothing on the exact solve, so it is funded at a limit of 100.0000 already; freeProjectSlack funds the same set at capex 100.0000 against 101.0000, leaving 1.0000 unspent.
why: Both free-project cases fund free + A for 70.0000; the extra million buys nothing.

prompt: An inventory is typed entirely in USD where million USD was meant. Why can a project-by-project check of risked EMV per million of capex never reveal the slip?
options: Both amounts sit in the same unit, so it cancels, and OK-1's 0.747917 would come out of a USD inventory unchanged.
The ratio prints to six decimals, which is too coarse to show a factor of a million between two inventories.
The engine converts USD to million USD before computing risked EMV, so every ratio is taken on corrected numbers.
The ratio divides by capex in grid cells, and a cell is the same size in either unit.
explanation: The engine holds no currency field, no unit field and no scale check, and the exact solve returns the same set in any unit, as the rawDollars case shows; a mixed inventory is the slip no ratio can catch.
why: No grid: a USD inventory solves to the same set. Copy rule: contrastive ("instead of", "rather than", ", never", ", not") reworded, meaning unchanged.

prompt: Risking every row by hand before solving, a candidate's value for one project differs from the explorer's risked EMV column. What causes does the method name?
options: Grid rounding, since the column shows EMV after capex is rounded to cells.
The simulation, since the column reports the mean of the seeded Monte Carlo draws, which never lands exactly on the hand line.
Correlation, which the explorer applies to each project's EMV before printing.
A mistyped input, or a default that fired: a pos left out read as 1, or a negative fail_cost read as 0.
explanation: A pos over 1, under 0, blank or non-numeric never reaches the column, because it is refused by project name. OK-3's hand line, 0.250000 x 420.0000 - 0.750000 x 85.0000 = 41.2500, matching the engine shows the row was read as typed.
why: pos out of range is refused; the key names only defaults and the fail_cost floor.

prompt: freeProjectZeroLimit and limitBelowEveryProject both run at a limit that no project with a cost can meet. Which of them returns a funded set, and why?
options: freeProjectZeroLimit, whose project costs 0.0000 and weighs nothing, so it is funded for 10.0000; below every project nothing fits.
limitBelowEveryProject, since a limit of 30.0000 funds part of A, and a fraction of a project is how a tight limit is used.
Both, since the engine relaxes a limit that no project can meet and funds the cheapest project it has.
Neither, since an empty set is the engine refusing a limit it cannot use, and no optimum exists for either input.
explanation: The engine funds the free project at a limit of 0.0000, which is the golden optimum; limitBelowEveryProject at 30.0000 funds nothing, capex 0.0000 and EMV 0.0000, because A costs 50.0000 and B 80.0000.
why: freeProjectZeroLimit funds the free project; only limitBelowEveryProject returns an empty set.

prompt: For the 450.0000 set the engine prints seed 20260829, iterations 10000, P(loss) 0.123600 and P90 -18.3574. Why does it show the seed?
options: Because the seed fixes the average correlation between projects, which is the one simulation input the risk summary has no other field to display.
So anyone can rerun the same simulation and reproduce its loss probability and percentiles exactly.
Because the loss probability is read from a normal approximation, and the seed records which version of that approximation the run applied.
Because the optimizer breaks ties with it, so another seed can fund another set.
explanation: The engine simulates success, failure and the success NPV of each project in every one of 10000 iterations from the seed, so the same seed and iterations reproduce P(loss) 0.123600 and P90 -18.3574 exactly.
why: Repair history stripped.

prompt: An analyst types OKONO's limit of 450.0000 million USD and every capex as counts of USD, keeping the NPVs in million USD. What in the output shows that anything changed?
options: A PortfolioInputError, since a capex in the hundreds of millions is outside the range the engine accepts and nothing is chosen.
A unit warning, since the engine compares the limit with the NPVs and flags an inventory typed at the wrong scale.
The solveMethod, which reads "grid-feasible" once the capex is typed in USD, since figures that large leave the exact solve.
Nothing: solved exactly on the capex as typed, it funds OK-1 + OK-3 + OK-4 again with solveMethod "exact", and the engine holds no unit field.
explanation: The published rawDollars case does the same with the classic inventory: limit 450000000.0000, A + B + D for 250.0000, solveMethod exact. The engine holds no currency or unit field, so a consistently scaled capex column is invisible and harmless.
why: Keyed resolution switch is false; the set comes back unchanged and option 2 was the truth.

prompt: Why does the engine refuse a capex of -150 outright, with no clamp to 0?
options: A negative capex turns the risked EMV negative, and the engine refuses any project whose risked EMV is 0 or less, the same way it refuses a negative capex.
The knapsack grid cannot store a negative weight, so the refusal protects the array the optimizer builds and says nothing about what the input means.
A clamp to 0 would charge the project a grid cell for nothing, and the engine refuses every input that would take capacity the project never asked for.
A project that pays you to fund it breaks the idea of a limit.
explanation: Capex never enters the risked EMV line, and a project with EMV of 0 or less is simply left out. The published message reads Project "B" has a negative capex (-150); capex must be 0 or more.
why: Repair history stripped from the prompt; contrastives removed.

prompt: A one in four exploration well has its chance of success typed correctly and its fail cost typed with a minus sign to show it is a loss. The run returns no error. How is the failure branch valued?
options: At nothing: a negative fail cost is read as 0, so a well like OK-3 would carry 105.0000, its success branch alone.
At twice the fail cost, since the minus sign typed in the field and the minus sign in the formula compound.
At its intended cost, because the engine takes the absolute value of a negative fail cost before it weights the branch.
It is never valued, since a negative fail cost is refused with the same error as a negative capex.
explanation: negativeFailCostIsZero returns 40.0000 for a fail cost of -30 at pos 0.5 on an npv_p50 of 80, the success branch alone. A pos typed as a percentage is caught: Project "Appraisal" has a pos outside 0 to 1 (30); pos must be a number from 0 to 1.
why: A pos typed as a percentage is refused; rebuilt on the fail_cost floor that still reads as 0.

prompt: Four inventories are run through the optimizer. Which one does the engine refuse outright?
options: One with a limit of 30.0000 that sits under every project, since no set can be built and the knapsack has nothing it can return.
One holding a project whose npv_p10 is entered below its npv_p90, since a success spread cannot be built from an inverted range.
One holding a project with a capex of -0.5.
One holding a project with fail_cost -30, since a loss typed below zero is outside the range the engine documents for fail_cost.
explanation: The negative capex is refused: Project "1" has a negative capex (-0.5); capex must be 0 or more. limitBelowEveryProject at 30.0000 funds nothing, inverted percentiles give a spread of 0.0000, and a fail_cost of -30 is read as 0.
why: pos 1.4 is refused too, so option 3 became a second right answer; replaced with an input still accepted.

prompt: The published gridOvershoot case has projects costing 4000.0000, 2002.0000 and 1995.0000 against a limit of 6000.0000. What does the engine return?
options: A PortfolioInputError, since two projects whose capex together pass the limit cannot be entered in one inventory.
A + C at capex 5995.0000 for 780.0000, solved exactly, with overLimit false and overLimitBy 0.0000.
A + B at capex 6002.0000 for 800.0000, flagged with overLimit true and overLimitBy 2.0000 for the reader to correct.
B + C at capex 3997.0000 for 580.0000, since the engine drops the largest project whenever a pair would breach the limit.
explanation: The exact solve never exceeds the limit: A + B would cost 6002.0000, so the best set that fits is A + C at 500.0000 plus 280.0000. overLimit and overLimitBy stay in every result and read false and 0.0000 on an exact solve.
why: gridOvershoot is solved exactly to A + C inside the limit.

prompt: Sorting OKONO by risked EMV per million USD and funding down the list at 450.0000 gives OK-1 + OK-4 + OK-5 for 287.7500. Why does the engine reach 291.0000?
options: It ranks by plain risked EMV and ignores the ratio, which puts the exploration well ahead of the workovers.
It risks each project again in the simulation, which marks down the workovers' certain success.
It compares combinations of whole projects, while a list judges projects one at a time and stops when the next one does not fit.
It uses a coarser grid than the hand list, and rounding lets the well's capex fit beside OK-1 and OK-4.
explanation: OKONO is solved exactly, solveMethod "exact" with optimalityGap 0.0000; the gain of 3.2500 comes from choosing the set, with no rounding or risk involved.
why: No grid. Copy rule: contrastive ("instead of", "rather than", ", never", ", not") reworded, meaning unchanged.

prompt: An exploration well is entered with an npv_p50 and a fail_cost, but the pos field is left out of the row entirely. How does the engine value it?
options: It refuses the row, since a project with no chance of success cannot be risked and the engine names the offending project in its error.
At the middle of the range, since a missing chance of success is read as a coin toss until a value between 0 and 1 is entered.
At its npv_p50 weighted by the average pos of the other projects, which is how the engine fills a chance nobody entered.
As a certain success worth its npv_p50, since an absent pos defaults to 1.
explanation: The published unrisked case enters no pos and no fail_cost and returns 250.0000, its whole npv_p50 of 250, so a well entered with no pos is counted as if it cannot fail. A pos typed as a blank is refused by name.
why: A blank pos is refused; only an omitted one defaults.

prompt: An appraisal well's row is saved with no pos field at all, and the optimizer values it at the default of 1. Where else does that default reach?
options: Nothing else, because the risk summary draws its own success rate from the entered percentiles and only the risked EMV line uses the default.
The seeded risk summary draws it as a success in every iteration, so its funded set looks safer as well as more valuable.
The seed, because the engine reseeds the simulation whenever a default fires, recording the correction.
The optimizer's method, because a defaulted row sends the solve to the fallback grid so it can be marked.
explanation: nullPosIsDefault returns 80.0000, a certain success, and at seed 20260829 over 10000 iterations such a project never contributes a failure to P(loss) or to the P90 low case. A pos typed as 1.4 is refused before anything runs.
why: pos 1.4 is refused; rebuilt on a pos left out, whose default does travel into the simulation.

prompt: The published posZero case enters pos 0 on npv_p50 80 and fail_cost 30, and returns -30.0000. What does that value describe?
options: A pos typed below the range and read as 0, since the engine holds every chance of success between 0 and 1.
The default of 1 applied to a pos it could not read, with the success branch then charged at the fail cost.
The absolute value of the fail cost taken as a gain, since a chance of 0 reverses the sign of the failure branch.
A certain failure worth -30.0000, minus its fail cost, since a pos of 0 is inside the range the engine accepts.
explanation: -(1 - 0) x 30 = -30.0000. A pos below 0 is refused: posBelowZeroRefused gives Project "a" has a pos outside 0 to 1 (-0.2); pos must be a number from 0 to 1.
why: posBelowZeroClamps is now posBelowZeroRefused; rebuilt on posZero, which is accepted.

prompt: At a limit of 750.0000 million USD the engine funds OK-1 + OK-2 + OK-3 + OK-4 + OK-5 for capex 690.0000. Why is the rest of the limit left unspent?
options: The optimizer holds back a reserve against the loss probability, sized from the simulated spread of the set it has just funded.
OK-6's risked EMV per million USD is the lowest left, and the optimizer stops at the first project whose ratio falls under its cut-off.
The grid is coarse at that limit and rounds each capex up, so the five projects fill every cell although their capex sums to 690.0000.
The only project left, OK-6, costs 310.0000, and the optimizer cannot fund part of a project.
explanation: 750.0000 - 690.0000 = 60.0000 is left, and OK-6 needs 310.0000; the knapsack is solved exactly, so nothing was rounded.
why: No grid.

prompt: The greedy set at 450.0000 is OK-1 + OK-4 + OK-5 for 287.7500, and the optimizer funds OK-1 + OK-3 + OK-4 for 291.0000. How does the project with the lowest ratio get into the best set?
options: It uses the 30.0000 the list left idle: 41.2500 on 90.0000 beats 38.0000 on 60.0000 once the whole limit counts.
The optimizer ranks by plain risked EMV, where OK-3's 41.2500 beats OK-5's 38.0000.
The optimizer credits the well with part of its success case of 420.0000, which the ratio leaves out.
The optimizer lets the limit stretch by one grid cell, giving OK-3 room the ranked list lacked.
explanation: Swapping the workovers for the well spends the last 30.0000 and gains 3.2500; the solve is exact at 450.0000, so no stretch or rounding is involved.
why: No grid.

prompt: In the published zeroEmvExcluded case a project with capex 30.0000 and risked EMV 0.0000 sits beside good at a limit of 500.0000. Why does the engine leave it out?
options: It adds nothing to the objective and still uses capex, so a risked EMV of 0 or less is never funded.
Its capex of 30.0000 cannot fit beside good, since a limit of 500.0000 is checked on a grid of the limit / 2000 per cell.
The engine rejects a zero risked EMV row as unfinished and returns an error naming it.
It would be funded under a tight limit, since a zero project is dropped only when money is left over and idle capex costs nothing.
explanation: The engine funds good alone for capex 50.0000 and risked EMV 30.0000 with 450.0000 of the limit spare, solved exactly.
why: No grid.

prompt: At 450.0000 the optimizer's set beats the greedy set by 3.2500. If a revision to one project's inputs closed that gap to an exact tie, what would decide which set came back?
options: The loss probability, since a tie hands the choice to the risk summary and it favours the workovers' certain success over the well.
The larger total success NPV, used by the optimizer as a second key, favouring the well.
The capex spent: the optimizer keeps the tied set with less capex, OK-1 + OK-4 + OK-5 at 420.0000, whatever the entry order.
The order the projects were entered in, since the first set built is kept against an equal one found later.
explanation: Among sets tied on risked EMV the exact solve keeps the one with less capex, and entry order decides only between sets of equal capex and equal EMV. The two sets here cost 450.0000 and 420.0000.
why: Tie rule: the lighter set wins a tie on risked EMV; entry order decides only at equal capex.

prompt: The OKONO frontier shows a step of 3.2500 three times, at points 2, 5 and 11. What is that step?
options: OK-3 added on top of the set before at a diluted ratio, since its 41.2500 is spread across the capex of the projects already funded.
Rounding residue the grid leaves between whole cells, repeated wherever a capex does not divide evenly into the cell size.
Three different small projects that each happen to be worth 3.2500 of risked EMV once their fail costs are charged.
The same swap each time: OK-5 out and OK-3 in, a net 3.2500 for a net 30.0000 of capex.
explanation: OK-3 adds 41.2500 for 90.0000 and OK-5 takes away 38.0000 for 60.0000. The solve is exact, so there is no rounding to leave a residue.
why: No grid.

prompt: The optimizer runs OKONO at a limit of 750.0000 million USD. Where does the frontier's last point sit, and why?
options: At 690.0000 and 444.0000, with 60.0000 unspent, because no remaining project fits and OK-6 alone costs 310.0000.
At 750.0000 and 444.0000, because the last point is always printed at the limit whatever its set costs.
At 1000.0000 and 588.0000, the value of all six projects, since a limit is rounded up to the next whole set.
At 690.0000 with a grid undershoot, the coarse rounding that leaves a set out, which a finer cell would recover.
explanation: A point is printed at what its set costs. OKONO is solved exactly, so the 60.0000 is genuine: OK-6 is the only project left and needs 310.0000.
why: No grid.

prompt: The published negativeEmvHugeBudget case has a limit of 10000.0000 and funds good + better for capex 120.0000 and risked EMV 75.0000. A third project, neg, would easily fit. Why is it left out?
options: The limit is above 5000, so a coarse grid charges neg more cells than its capex of 20.0000 and it cannot fit beside the others.
Its risked EMV is -44.0000, and funding it would lower the summed risked EMV by exactly that amount.
